opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think those results are really telling, and honestly they line up with what a lot of us suspected for a while. The way I see it, attention and state space models do fundamentally different things. A recurrent model like Mamba compresses the whole history into a fixed-size state. That makes it great at the bulk of sequence processing: tracking context, modeling local and medium-range structure, and doing it efficiently. Attention keeps a full cache of everything it's seen, so it's very good at precise retrieval, like looking back and pulling out an exact token or fact.

What the hybrid findings suggest is that you don't need that exact-retrieval mechanism at every layer. You need a little of it, placed in the right spots. The recurrent layers can do most of the heavy lifting, and a handful of global attention layers act almost like a lookup or memory-access module. When people find they can also share KV caches across those attention layers, it reinforces the point. The information those layers need to retrieve is fairly redundant, so you don't need many independent copies of the full history.

There are a few takeaways for me. The first is practical. The KV cache is the main memory bottleneck for long-context inference, so cutting the number of attention layers and then sharing their caches compounds the savings. You get much better throughput and much longer contexts without giving up much quality.

The second is more conceptual. It's evidence that the "attention is all you need" framing was always a bit of an overstatement. Attention is one very useful primitive, but it's an expensive one, and models seem to use it fairly sparsely when given the choice. That tells me we should think of architectures as compositions of primitives with different strengths, not as a single mechanism stacked over and over.

The third is that it points to open questions I find exciting. Why do models need exact retrieval at all, and how much? Can we design recurrent layers whose states are expressive enough that we need even fewer attention layers? Or are there better hybrid structures than just interleaving layers, like attention that's more selective about what it caches? I don't think the current ratios people land on are fundamental. They reflect where our recurrent layers are today. As the state-based layers get stronger, I'd expect the share of attention to keep shrinking. Still, I suspect some form of explicit memory access will stay useful, and figuring out the minimal, cleanest way to provide it is a really interesting design problem.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent models compress the whole history into a fixed-size state, but does not propose storing a small representation of every past token or claim that this preserves the ability to remember the entire history.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I take away is that it's a confirmation of something we've suspected for a while, which is that attention is doing a very specific job, and you don't need very much of it. When we first started mixing SSM layers with attention layers, the kind of folk result was that you only needed something like one in six or one in eight layers to be attention to recover essentially full quality on things like retrieval and in-context learning. And now people are pushing that even further, and on top of that finding that the attention layers that remain can share a single KV cache, and it still basically works.

So what does that tell you? I think it tells you that the bulk of what a language model is doing, the "compute" part, the compression and the processing of context into some kind of state, is well-served by these recurrent, fixed-size-state layers. And then what attention is actually providing is a kind of precise lookup capability, a way to go back and copy or retrieve exact tokens from the context. That's a very different function from the rest of the model, and it's a function that you only need to do in a few places. Once you've done the lookup, the rest of the network can just carry that information forward in its state.

The KV cache sharing result is interesting to me for a slightly different reason. It suggests that the keys and values across those attention layers are pretty redundant, that the model doesn't really need many different "views" of the raw context, it needs one good one. And that has really nice systems implications, because the KV cache is the thing that dominates memory at inference time for long contexts. If you've gone from thirty-two attention layers down to four, and those four share a cache, you've cut your memory footprint by something like an order of magnitude or more, and you're starting to look a lot like a pure recurrent model from a deployment perspective while keeping the capabilities that attention gives you.

The more conceptual takeaway, though, and this is the thing I actually find exciting, is that it reframes the question. For a long time the debate was framed as attention versus SSMs, like one of these has to win. And I think what these results say is that that was never the right framing. They're complementary primitives. One is a compressed state that's great for building up a representation, and the other is a lossless memory that you occasionally need to reach into. The right architecture uses as little of the expensive one as it can get away with, and the empirical answer seems to be: a lot less than we were using.

And I'd push a little further and say we probably still don't understand what the minimal amount is, or what those remaining attention layers are really doing mechanistically. If you can share the cache, maybe you can compress it too. Maybe the right abstraction is something in between, a state that's larger than a Mamba state but doesn't grow linearly with context. I think that middle ground is where a lot of the interesting architecture work is going to be over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response discusses recurrent fixed-size state for processing context and speculates about a larger state that does not grow linearly with context. It does not propose storing a small representation of every past token to preserve memory of the entire history.

astra-6.text:
I think the main takeaway is that you don’t necessarily need global attention at every layer to get the benefits of attention. In a hybrid, you can let the other sequence-modeling layers do much of the processing, and use attention selectively where access to the full context is useful.

Sharing KV caches suggests there may also be redundancy in what those attention layers store. That’s interesting because the cache is a major memory cost during generation. If you can reduce the number of distinct caches while maintaining quality, that’s a meaningful efficiency gain.

But I’d distinguish that empirical result from saying attention is unnecessary. To me, it points toward a question about division of labor: what should be compressed into a state, and what needs to remain available for direct retrieval? The interesting thing about hybrids is that you can make that tradeoff rather than asking one mechanism to do everything.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compressing information into a state and reducing distinct attention caches, but does not propose that a small representation of every past token can preserve the model’s ability to remember its entire history.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main takeaway is that you don’t necessarily need global attention at every layer. In a hybrid model, the other layers can handle a lot of the sequence processing, and attention can provide access to information that needs to be retrieved more explicitly. If you can also share the KV cache across attention layers, that suggests there’s some redundancy in what those layers are storing.

That’s exciting because the KV cache is a major memory cost during inference, especially as the context grows. So there’s an opportunity to retain the benefits of attention while making the model much more efficient. But I’d be careful about interpreting that as saying attention is unnecessary. The interesting question is where you need it, how much you need, and whether those answers hold across different tasks and context lengths.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sharing KV caches to reduce inference memory, but does not propose that a small representation of every past token can preserve the model’s ability to remember its entire history.
